title: Pulling the carpet below the learner’s feet: Genetic algorithm to learn ensemble machine learning model during concept drift
short_title: Pulling the carpet: genetic algorithm ensembles for concept drift

abstract: Data-driven models, in general, and machine learning (ML) models, in particular, have gained popularity over recent years with an increased usage of such models across the scientific and engineering domains. When using ML models in realistic and dynamic environments, users often need to handle the challenge of concept drift (CD). In this study, we explore the application of genetic algorithms (GAs) to address the challenges posed by CD in such settings. Formally, we propose a novel two-level ensemble ML model, which combines a global ML model with a CD detector, operating as an aggregator for a population of ML pipeline models, each one with an adjusted CD detector by itself responsible for re-training its ML model. In addition, we show that one can further improve the proposed model by utilizing off-the-shelf automatic ML (AutoML) methods. Through extensive synthetic dataset analysis, we show that the proposed model statistically significantly outperforms an ML pipeline with a CD algorithm, particularly in scenarios with unknown CD characteristics or a mixture of moving and shifting CDs. Moreover, we show a sub-linear decline in the proposed method’s performance with respect to a higher drifting rate and robustness to the underlying AutoML method utilized.
summary: Machine learning models used in changing environments face concept drift, where the patterns in the data shift over time. We propose a two-level ensemble built with a genetic algorithm: a global model with a drift detector aggregates a population of machine learning pipelines, each with its own drift detector that triggers retraining. On synthetic datasets, it statistically significantly outperformed a single pipeline with a drift algorithm, especially when drift characteristics were unknown or mixed.
key_findings: The ensemble combines a global model and drift detector with a population of pipelines, each retraining its own model when drift is detected.
Off-the-shelf automatic machine learning (AutoML) methods can further improve the proposed model.
The model statistically significantly outperformed a pipeline with a drift algorithm, particularly with unknown drift characteristics or mixed moving and shifting drifts.
Performance declined sub-linearly as the drifting rate increased and was robust to the AutoML method used.
